Passive iFIR filters for data-driven velocity control in robotics
Yi Zhang1, Zixing Wang1, and Fulvio Forni1
Abstract— We present a passive, data-driven velocity control
method for nonlinear robotic manipulators that achieves better
tracking performance than optimized PID with comparable
design complexity. Using only three minutes of probing data,
a VRFT-based design identifies passive iFIR controllers that
(i) preserve closed-loop stability via passivity constraints and
(ii) outperform a VRFT-tuned PID baseline on the Franka
Research 3 robot in both joint-space and Cartesian-space
velocity control, achieving up to a 74.5% reduction in tracking
error for the Cartesian velocity tracking experiment with
the most demanding reference model. When the robot end-
effector dynamics change, the controller can be re-learned from
new data, regaining nominal performance. This study bridges
learning-based control and stability-guaranteed design: passive
iFIR learns from data while retaining passivity-based stability
guarantees, unlike many learning-based approaches.
I. INTRODUCTION
Learning-based control has made impressive progress in
robotics, enabling manipulators to acquire complex behaviors
directly from data when accurate models are unavailable or
hard to derive. Deep reinforcement learning policies can in
principle represent rich control laws that adapt to unknown
dynamics and contact conditions. However, these methods
typically require large amounts of data and often abandon
formal guarantees of stability or robustness [1].
In practice, proportional–integral–derivative (PID) con-
trollers remain the standard in industrial manipulators due
to their simplicity and ease of deployment. Yet PID requires
tuning, and its three-parameter structure is too limited to
shape the closed-loop response arbitrarily, especially for
high-order dynamics. This leaves a gap between simple but
limited classical controllers and expressive but fragile data-
driven ones. Developing controllers that are learnable from
data while providing stability guarantees remains a central
challenge for the learning and robotics communities.
This paper argues that passive iFIR controllers [2], [3]
offer a middle ground. An iFIR controller extends PID with
a finite impulse response (FIR) term that provides a richer
temporal representation while preserving a simple linear
structure. Using virtual reference feedback tuning (VRFT)
[4], the iFIR parameters can be learned directly from a
small batch of experimental data to approximate a desired
closed-loop response, without requiring an explicit model of
the robot and heavy computation. Passivity constraints are
imposed on the iFIR controller directly, and hence guarantee
closed-loop stability when interconnected with a passive

Velocity control plays a central role in modern robotic
manipulators, serving as the key interface between low-level
actuation and high-level motion generation. Industrial robots
typically execute commands through an internal velocity
loop because regulating velocity directly ensures smoothness,
robustness, and inherent damping [5]. Applications such as
polishing, welding, and machining demand precise control of
end-effector velocity along desired paths while maintaining
stability under model uncertainty [6].
Motivated by this, we use joint- and Cartesian-space ve-
locity control on a Franka Research 3 as our benchmark. We
show experimentally that passive iFIR learned from probing
data outperforms optimized PID and remains stable under
dynamics changes. We demonstrate:
1)Stability: passivity constraints applied to the iFIR
controller ensure stability of the closed-loop system;
2)Performance: passive iFIR control significantly reduce
tracking error compared to optimized PID, especially
in cases where end-effector dynamics are high-order
and the reference model is demanding;
3)Adaptability: when dynamics vary, a new controller
can be relearned in minutes with new probing data.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first instance where
passive iFIR controllers have been experimentally validated
in a robotic setting.
Section II reviews different types of controllers for robot
manipulators. Section III introduces the velocity control
problem we tackle. Section IV presents the passive iFIR
synthesis, with new results for the multiple-input multiple-
output (MIMO) setting. Section V shows the results of joint-
space velocity control of a Franka arm. Section VI extends
the evaluation to Cartesian-space velocity control. Section
VII discusses limitations and future work.
II. RELATED WORK
Robot manipulators still mainly rely on PID controllers
for their intuitive structure and ease of implementation [7].
Beyond classical tuning methods (e.g., Ziegler-Nichols and
Cohen-Coon), previous studies have looked at intelligent
tuning by utilizing fuzzy control [8], learning-assisted tun-
ing [9], and population-based optimization algorithms [10].
Despite its effectiveness and ubiquity, PID control offers
only three degrees of freedom, which limits the performance
of the closed-loop response, especially when the system
dynamics are high-order and nonlinear.
From the perspective of learning-based control, feedfor-
ward and recurrent neural networks have been used ex-arXiv:2603.29882v1  [cs.RO]  31 Mar 2026

tensively to compensate for uncertain robot arm dynamics
and improve tracking performance [11], [12], [13]. Simi-
larly, reinforcement learning (RL) has proven effective in
discovering control policies capable of managing the com-
plex dynamics inherent in robot manipulation. Such data-
driven methods can automatically improve control policies
by learning from experience, allowing robots to handle tasks
and environments that are difficult to model. Learning-based
methods have demonstrated strong performance in robotic
control, but a significant drawback is that vanilla learning-
based controllers generally lack formal stability guarantees
[1]. A learned policy may appear effective in training or
simulations yet exhibit unstable behavior when encountering
novel situations. There are efforts from the learning commu-
nity to build safe policies. For example, Lyapunov-guided
RL builds Lyapunov functions into local constraints, and
policy is obtained by solving a constrained Markov decision
process [14], [15]. However, most of these approaches only
satisfy safety level I [16], where constraint satisfaction is
encouraged but not guaranteed and stability is typically
verified empirically.
Passivity-based control [17] leverages energy-dissipation
inequalities to guarantee robust stability. Because the
negative-feedback interconnection of passive systems is itself
passive [18], [19], [20], a passive controller can be coupled
with a robot to ensure stability, even when the robot model
is not accurate. This framework extends to environmental
interactions: since most physical environments are passive,
the robot remains stable during contact despite environmental
uncertainties. Recent learning-based manipulation controllers
exploit this idea by constraining the learned policy to remain
passive through monitoring and limiting energy injection
[21], [22]. In contrast, our data-driven approach synthesizes
controllers that are passive by construction. By formulating
the problem as a constrained optimization, we identify the
passive controller that optimizes performance given the data.
Velocity control is a natural testbed for our approach and
a core component of many industrial robot architectures.
Most manipulators implement a two-loop structure: an inner
joint-velocity loop with an outer position or task-space
loop. This architecture is theoretically well established. [5]
analyzes the two-loop design and provides conditions for
global exponential stability. [23] provides a theoretical and
empirical comparison of velocity, acceleration, and force-
based operational-space controllers, reporting that velocity-
based controllers are straightforward to deploy but large
gains and noisy velocity measurements can lead to excessive
damping or even instability, which highlights the importance
of shaping the effective velocity-loop dynamics. For these
reasons, we adopt joint- and Cartesian-space velocity control
as representative benchmarks to evaluate tracking perfor-
mance and robustness of the proposed controllers.
III. PROBLEM STATEMENT
We study velocity control of a seven-degree-of-freedom
robot manipulator with revolute joints under different load
dynamics, considering two common interfaces:(i) Joint-space velocity control (single joint):given a
desired joint velocity trajectoryv∗(t)∈Rfor all timet, the
controller outputs a torqueu(t)∈Rto regulate the joint
velocityv(t).
(ii) Cartesian-space velocity control:given a desired
end-effector velocityv∗
ee(t)∈R3for all timet, the controller
outputs joint torquesu(t)∈R7to regulate the end-effector
velocityv ee(t).
As shown in the block diagram of Fig. 1, the manipulator
is considered as a plantPmapping generalized force inputs
u(i.e. torques in our case) into velocity outputsy(joint or
Cartesian). The controller is denoted byC. A user-specified
reference modelM rencodes the desired transient behavior
of the controlled robot. Our goal is to shape the closed-
loop response of the robot to approximate, as closely as
possible, the reference responseM rwhile ensuring closed-
loop stability. For simplicity, experiments are limited to first-
and second-order linear time-invariant reference models.
Extensions to larger reference models are straightforward.
Closed-loop stability is guaranteed by enforcing controller
passivity, provided the sampling frequency is high enough to
mitigate discretization effects. Physical dissipation ensures
that uncontrolled manipulators are output-strict passive from
inpututo velocity outputy[20], [19], while the zero-
order hold implementation of the control action introduces a
shortage of passivity proportional to the sampling period. Ac-
cording to the passivity theorem and under mild detectability
assumptions, asymptotic stability is preserved if this effect
is compensated by the system’s dissipation [20], [24]. For
a sufficiently high control frequency, the parasitic energy
generated by discretization is dominated by the combination
of the robot’s internal damping and the controller’s virtual
dissipation, thereby preserving the passivity, and thus the
stability, of the closed-loop system. We refer to [25] for a
more comprehensive approach to passivity-preserving inter-
connections between continuous and discrete systems.

V. JOINT SPACE VELOCITY CONTROL
A. Experimental setting and performance metrics
The experimental setup of the system is illustrated in
Fig. 3. A flexible wood strip is driven by the built-in
motor at the last joint of the Franka Research 3 robot with
joint torques commanded vialibfrankaat 1 kHz. We
consider two loads: a long plate (Fig. 3a) and a shorter plate
(Fig. 3b). The flexibility of the plate introduces high-order,
poorly modeled dynamics, which makes accurate velocity
control challenging. This configuration is representative of

tasks, where the robot manipulates payloads that behave as

C. Robust tracking and retraining
We test both PID and iFIR controllers designed for the
case of Fig. 3a on the perturbed load of Fig. 3b. We considerthe same batch of tests of Section V-B. Without retraining,
as expected, both closed loops exhibit degraded tracking
performance (Fig. 4b). Notably, even in this perturbed case,
the iFIR controller achieved a closer match to the reference
model and reduced overshoot.
Because iFIR controller training is fast, performance can
be further improved by collecting data under the new load
conditions and rapidly retraining both controllers. The results
after retraining are shown in Fig. 4c. NRMSE values are
summarized in Table I. After retraining, both controllers
exhibit similar behavior, with a modest improvement of -
3.2% in favor of PID. This indicates that both designs achieve
comparable performance for simpler load dynamics.
D. Passivity and stability
To highlight the importance of stability guarantee provided
by the passivity constraints, we redesign the iFIR controller
of Fig. 3a adopting a more aggressive reference model,
represented in the Laplace domain byM r(s) =100
s2+6s+100.
We design three controllers: a passive iFIR, an iFIR learned
without passivity constraints, and a PID baseline. The iFIR

designed without passivity constraints is non-passive (by
testing its Nyquist diagram) and leads unstable closed-loop
behavior in most test cases. As shown in Fig. 5, the non-
passive iFIR closed loop shows growing oscillations that
eventually trigger joint velocity safety limits, whereas the
passive iFIR and PID controllers remain stable. The non-
passive iFIR provides an example of an arbitrary learned
controller optimized over costs that do not offer stability
guarantees. In our setting, enforcing passivity is critical for
maintaining stability under demanding reference dynamics.

VI. CARTESIAN SPACE VELOCITY CONTROL
A. SISO Cartesian velocity control
In many manipulation tasks, end-effector motion is most
naturally specified in Cartesian space. We investigate Carte-
sian velocity control on the Franka Research 3 robot without
any additional end-effector load. We focus on a local operat-
ing region where training and testing are performed near the
same configuration, and compare PID and iFIR controllers
under both SISO and MIMO designs.
We first consider the simplest Cartesian controller struc-
ture, where each velocity axis is regulated independently by
a SISO controller. Letr iandv idenote the reference and
measured Cartesian velocity along the three axesi∈ {x,y,z}.

B. MIMO Cartesian velocity control
The use of separate controllers on each axis is suboptimal
as the manipulator Cartesian dynamics are coupled, through
non-diagonal task-space inertia and Coriolis terms: torques
applied to correct one axis induce motion along all other
axes [27]. This motivates the development of a 3×3 MIMO
iFIR controller, operating on the full set of axes at the same
time.

Section VI-A. Training the MIMO iFIR controller of order
200 takes 298s. A MIMO PID controller is also trained for
comparison. Its proportional, integral, and derivative ‘gains’
are now 3×3 positive definite matrices.
Results are reported in Fig. 6b and Table II. In the MIMO
setting, both PID and iFIR perform better than in the SISO
case of Section VI-A. Both follow the first-order reference
reasonably well over the identified bandwidth, with the iFIR
achieving superior tracking performance. A clearer difference
arises when the same controllers are evaluated at an end-
effector position away from the training point, as shown
in Fig. 7. While performance degrades for both, the PID
response develops noticeable high-frequency oscillations in
all directions, possibly caused by overly aggressive gains.
Overall, PID and iFIR perform similarly near the train-
ing configuration, but iFIR degrades more gracefully under
operating-point shifts.

Cartesian-space velocity control validated experimentally on
a Franka Research 3 manipulator. We have shown that

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel passive, data-driven velocity control method for robotic manipulators. The key contributions and main points covered are:

*   **Passive iFIR Controllers:** The paper proposes using passive Infinite Impulse Response (iFIR) controllers, which extend traditional PID controllers with a finite impulse response term. This structure allows for richer temporal representation while maintaining a simple linear form.
*   **Data-Driven Design:** The iFIR controller parameters are learned directly from experimental data using Virtual Reference Feedback Tuning (VRFT). This approach avoids the need for an explicit robot model and complex computations.
*   **Guaranteed Stability:** A core feature is the enforcement of passivity constraints on the iFIR controller. This ensures closed-loop stability when the controller is interconnected with a passive robot and environment, unlike many other learning-based control methods.
*   **Superior Performance:** Experimental results on a Franka Research 3 robot demonstrate that the passive iFIR controllers achieve significantly better tracking performance than optimized PID controllers, with up to a 74.5% reduction in tracking error in demanding scenarios.
*   **Adaptability:** The controller can be quickly re-learned from new data if the robot's dynamics change, regaining nominal performance.
*   **Bridging Learning and Stability:** The work aims to bridge the gap between expressive learning-based control and formal stability guarantees, offering a middle ground between simple but limited classical controllers and complex but potentially unstable data-driven approaches.
*   **Application to Velocity Control:** The method is specifically applied and evaluated for both joint-space and Cartesian-space velocity control, highlighting its practical relevance in industrial robotics.

structure.title: RELATED WORK
structure.summary: This partial document discusses data-driven approaches for robot control, focusing on velocity control. It highlights the limitations of traditional learning-based methods, particularly their lack of formal stability guarantees. The document then introduces passivity-based control as a framework that inherently ensures robust stability, even with uncertain robot dynamics or environmental interactions. It proposes a novel data-driven approach that synthesizes controllers that are passive by construction, formulated as a constrained optimization problem. The document also details the problem statement for velocity control of a seven-degree-of-freedom robot manipulator, considering both joint-space and Cartesian-space velocity control. It outlines the goal of shaping the closed-loop response to approximate a reference model while ensuring stability through controller passivity, especially in the context of discrete-time implementations. Finally, it introduces the iFIR (infinite impulse response filter) controller structure, leveraging its equivalence to positive realness for efficient passivity enforcement.

nodes.title: iFIR controller structure
nodes.summary: This partial document describes an iFIR (integral Finite Impulse Response) controller, which is a MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) discrete-time linear time-invariant system. It is presented as an alternative to PID controllers, replacing the derivative component with a FIR filter for smoother control. The document details the synthesis of iFIR controller coefficients using data-driven optimization, specifically through Virtual Reference Feedback Tuning (VRFT). This involves choosing a reference model, probing the system with generic inputs to collect data, and then solving an optimization problem to find the controller parameters. A key focus is on ensuring the stability and passivity of the iFIR controller. The document introduces conditions and a theorem related to passivity guarantees, involving constraints on the integral and FIR filter coefficients, and a method for approximating the positive realness condition of the FIR filter through finite sampling. The generalization of this data-driven passive iFIR controller design from SISO to MIMO systems and its validation with real-world robotic experiments are highlighted.

nodes.title: iFIR controller synthesis
nodes.summary:
The document discusses the iFIR (integrator Finite Impulse Response) controller, a type of MIMO discrete-time linear time-invariant system. It explains the controller's structure as a parallel interconnection of a MIMO integrator and a MIMO FIR filter, highlighting its replacement of PID's derivative component with a FIR filter for smoother control. The document details the synthesis of iFIR controller coefficients using data-driven optimization, specifically Virtual Reference Feedback Tuning (VRFT). This process involves defining a reference model, probing the system with generic inputs to collect data, and then solving an optimization problem to minimize the error between the controller output and the desired response.

A significant portion of the text is dedicated to ensuring the passivity of iFIR controllers, crucial for stability guarantees. It presents Theorem 1, which outlines conditions for passivity based on the controller's parameters, including constraints on the integrator gain (Γ) and the FIR filter coefficients (Hk). These constraints involve ensuring the integral action is passive and the FIR filter's impulse response decays exponentially. The theorem provides a method to obtain a passive iFIR controller through constrained optimization, trading off fitting performance for guaranteed passivity.

Finally, the document describes an experimental setup for joint space velocity control using a Franka Research 3 robot manipulating flexible wood strips. It compares the performance of the proposed passive iFIR controller with a passive PID controller, both optimized using VRFT. Performance is evaluated using the Normalized Root-Mean-Square Error (NRMSE) metric, and the improvement of the iFIR controller over the PID baseline is quantified. The experimental section details specific configurations, including controller orders, operating frequencies, and reference model characteristics.

structure.title: JOINT SPACE VELOCITY CONTROL
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt discusses the theoretical and experimental aspects of designing and implementing a passive iFIR controller.

**Main points covered:**

*   **Theoretical guarantees for passivity:** The document presents mathematical inequalities (equations 5b and 5c) that demonstrate the existence of a passive iFIR controller for any given angle $\theta$ and establishes a condition ($\epsilon \ge \frac{m-1}{M\pi}\frac{\rho_0}{1-\rho^m}\frac{1}{1-\rho}$) for the controller to guarantee non-negative feedback ($F(\theta) \ge 0$).
*   **Graphical interpretation of Theorem 1:** Figure 2 visually explains how Theorem 1 relates to finding an optimal passive iFIR controller by considering the trade-off between fitting performance and passivity within a constrained optimization problem.
*   **Problem formulation and optimization:** It's stated that the problem of finding the iFIR controller can be formulated as a convex optimization problem. This involves pre-computing data-dependent terms, a quadratic cost function, and constraints representable as linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). A relaxation of these constraints to linear inequalities is also mentioned for computational efficiency.
*   **Experimental setup for velocity control:** Section V details an experimental setup using a Franka Research 3 robot arm to control the velocity of a flexible wood strip. This setup is designed to mimic practical scenarios involving compliant or swinging payloads.
*   **Performance metrics:** The document defines two key metrics for evaluating controller performance:
    *   **NRMSE (Normalized Root-Mean-Square Error):** A standard metric to quantify reference tracking performance by comparing the measured response to the desired closed-loop response.
    *   **Improvement:** A metric to directly compare the performance of the iFIR controller against a passive PID controller, expressed as a percentage improvement.
*   **Nominal tracking experiment:** A specific experimental case (Fig. 3a) is described, detailing the parameters of the passive iFIR controller (order, operating frequency, memory) and the PID baseline. The chosen reference model is a first-order system with specific rise time, settling time, and bandwidth characteristics.

structure.title: CARTESIAN SPACE VELOCITY CONTROL
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the application of iFIR (infinite impulse response) controllers for robot velocity control, comparing them to traditional PID controllers. Key points covered include:

*   **Passivity and Stability:** The importance of passivity constraints in controller design is highlighted. Non-passive controllers, even if optimized for cost, can lead to unstable closed-loop behavior, as demonstrated by growing oscillations in test cases. Passive controllers, including passive iFIR and PID, are shown to maintain stability.
*   **Cartesian Space Velocity Control:** The document investigates Cartesian velocity control for a Franka Research 3 robot.
    *   **SISO (Single-Input, Single-Output) Design:** Each velocity axis (x, y, z) is controlled independently. The iFIR controller is trained and evaluated against a PID controller, showing superior performance in both time and frequency domains.
    *   **MIMO (Multiple-Input, Multiple-Output) Design:** A 3x3 MIMO iFIR controller is developed to account for the coupled dynamics of the robot's Cartesian space. This is compared to a MIMO PID controller.
*   **Performance Evaluation:** Controllers are evaluated using time-domain tracking of various velocity profiles (random-like, trapezoidal) and frequency-response analysis with sinusoidal references.
*   **Robustness to Operating Point Shifts:** The iFIR controller demonstrates more graceful degradation in performance when evaluated at an end-effector position away from the training configuration, compared to the PID controller which can develop high-frequency oscillations.
*   **Performance under Demanding Dynamics:** When subjected to a stricter second-order reference model, the iFIR controller significantly outperforms the PID controller in tracking accuracy, exhibiting less overshoot and phase lag.
*   **Conclusion:** The document concludes that passive iFIR controllers are a viable alternative to PID control for both joint- and Cartesian-space velocity control.

structure.title: CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
structure.summary: The document discusses the application of passive iFIR (infinite impulse response) controllers for robot manipulator velocity control in both joint and Cartesian spaces. It highlights the critical importance of passivity constraints for ensuring closed-loop stability, demonstrating that non-passive controllers, even when optimized for performance, can lead to instability. The paper compares the performance of passive iFIR controllers against traditional PID controllers in various scenarios, including Single-Input Single-Output (SISO) and Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) Cartesian velocity control. Experimental results on a Franka Research 3 robot show that passive iFIR controllers generally outperform PID controllers, especially under demanding reference dynamics and when operating away from the training configuration. The document also outlines limitations of the current approach, such as the reliance on hand-chosen reference models and the linear nature of the controllers, and suggests future work on automatic reference model derivation and nonlinear, adaptive iFIR controllers.

structure.title: REFERENCES
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a data-driven control method called passive iFIR for robot manipulators. The key points covered are:

*   **Performance and Advantages:** The proposed method, passive iFIR, can learn controllers with modest computational resources that satisfy passivity constraints and outperform traditional PID controllers tuned with VRFT, especially for demanding target dynamics and high-order end-effector dynamics. It achieves significant reductions in tracking error across various scenarios (joint-space, Cartesian-space, SISO/MIMO) and demonstrates improved robustness to dynamic changes and configurations. Enforcing passivity is highlighted as crucial for preventing instability.
*   **Limitations:** The current design approach is limited by the manual selection of the reference model, which can lead to infeasible targets or issues with stiction. The implementation does not adapt online, and it is a linear design, which has limitations in handling the nonlinearities of robot manipulators.
*   **Future Work:** The authors plan to focus on automatically deriving reference models and developing nonlinear, adaptive iFIR controllers.
*   **References:** A comprehensive list of references is provided, covering topics such as reinforcement learning with guarantees, data-driven control, virtual reference feedback tuning, robot motion control, friction compensation, PID control, neural network control for robots, safe reinforcement learning, and passivity-based control.
